Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: Explore every way of choosing M objects from a set of N.
How to play: Change N and M with the steppers and watch how many rows the list has.

Objects N 5 Choose M 3
Look for the math

Choosing three of five objects feels manageable. Choosing ten of twenty produces over a hundred and eighty thousand rows — and the counting rule explains exactly why.

The binomial coefficient

The number of ways to choose m objects from n is C(n, m) = n! / (m! (n − m)!). It is symmetric, C(n, m) = C(n, n − m), because choosing which to take is the same as choosing which to leave. It also obeys Pascal's rule: C(n, m) + C(n, m+1) = C(n+1, m+1). The logic test checks both identities across the whole option range.

Listing in order

The applet's list is in lexicographic order: it starts at 0, 1, …, m−1 internally, then repeatedly pushes the rightmost entry that still has room and resets the entries after it. A BigInteger countdown keeps track of how many rows are left. This port uses the same step, and the logic test compares every row with an independent recursive generator for all n ≤ 8, over 300 rows in all. The longest list here, C(20, 10) = 184,756, is counted and started but only its first thousand rows are drawn.

What the check found

Every generated row is distinct, sorted, inside 1..n, and in the same order as the independent generator; the countdown lands exactly on zero after C(n, m) rows. The applet's own about-box calls it a "Permutation Explorer", a leftover from a sibling applet — the rows here are combinations, where order does not matter.

Set N to 8 and M to 4. How many rows are there, and what happens if you set M to 5 instead?
